passage: Medieval European maps called mappae mundi often placed Jerusalem at the center of the world and filled their margins with biblical scenes and imagined creatures. Modern viewers sometimes conclude that their makers knew little geography. But many of the same monasteries that produced these maps also kept detailed written itineraries listing towns, rivers, and the distances between them for travelers. This suggests that mappae mundi ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: were probably intended to express religious and cultural ideas rather than to guide travel.
were made by monks who had never traveled beyond their own monasteries and so knew little about geography.
were more accurate than modern maps in showing the distances between towns.
were replaced by written itineraries because travelers found them confusing.
steps: The same makers had accurate travel itineraries, so ignorance of geography doesn't explain the maps.
The maps' religious center and biblical scenes point to a different purpose.
So the maps likely expressed beliefs rather than serving as travel guides.
The text says nothing about the monks' travel, map accuracy versus modern maps, or one form replacing the other.
key: When evidence rules out one explanation, infer the alternative the details point to.
